body_markdown: My wife and I call our 1968 Buick Riviera “The Aqua Zephyr” because it looks like a turquoise breeze as she floats down the road. On July 10, 1968, a fellow named Ralph Marino purchased this[Riviera](https://www.hagerty.com/valuation-tools/buick/riviera/1968/1968-buick-riviera-base?id=aCn1I000000DUCVSA4) new from Skip Erb Buick in Akron, Ohio. I like to imagine that this Riviera, painted a rare Aqua Mist—a one-year-only GM shade that fewer than 3% of ’68 Rivieras received—was sitting on the dealership’s showroom floor when Mr. Marino came to the lot looking to purchase a new Buick. The color would have been so eye-catching, compared to the whites and earth tones so prevalent during that period, that he could not resist the temptation to stroll over and look at the car. Whatever the circumstances of his visit to Skip Erb Buick that day, Mr. Marino went home with a brand-new Riviera that had only been built in the second week of May. He owned this car for the next 33 years, and included in its documentation is a copy of the Ohio title with registration date stamps from 1968 to the mid-1980s. Mike Sumrell In 2001, Mr. Marino sold the Buick to his niece and her husband in Raleigh, North Carolina. It stayed with them until December 2015, when she sold it on Craigslist to a gentleman from Vass, North Carolina. By this time, this Riviera was suffering from advanced road salt rust in the lower fenders and rocker panels, as well as rust under the vinyl top and in the trunk area. The third owner never registered the Buick in his name but spent the majority of 2016 repairing the rust damage and repainting the body and roof while also replacing the black vinyl top. The final result was a beautifully repainted Riv in its original color. I happened to spot this Riviera for sale on the Fayetteville, NC, Craigslist in May 2017. At the time, I owned a white 1969 Chevrolet Caprice Sport Sedan four-door hardtop. Although I loved the long, open lines and excellent 360-degree driving visibility of the car, it definitely lacked any eye-catching pizzazz due to its “grocery getter” styling and medium green interior color (commonly referred to as “baby-poo green”). So I wanted something to replace the Caprice, which we had dubbed “The White Stallion.” I was mesmerized by[the Riviera](https://www.hagerty.com/media/automotive-history/the-1995-99-buick-riviera-ended-the-premium-personal-luxury-era/) pictures in the online ad. They showed a gorgeous turquoise-and-black Buick. I showed the ad to my wife, who was also impressed with the Buick’s lines and color combination, and she agreed with me that we needed to go look at this car, since it was not too far from where we live. So we did. Mike Sumrell Mike Sumrell We took it for a test drive and were impressed with how well it drove and how good it looked. Even the air conditioning worked, which is a must in summertime North Carolina. We gave the owner $1000 to hold the car for a week while we got our finances in order. We made arrangements to meet the owner again at his home and pay the balance, and he informed us that an agent for an interested party in Australia was due to visit the next day to look at the car. I drove the car home feeling ecstatic that we had purchased it “just in time.” During our ownership, I have replaced the Buick’s points with a Pertronix electronic ignition, made new trunk mats, and had the original radiator re-cored. I also had a new quick-ratio power steering box installed and replaced the original carburetor and alternator with date-correct rebuilt units. The car now has rebuilt front and rear suspension with new shocks, and I replaced most of the rubber vacuum hoses for the hide-away headlights and the HVAC system. The instrument panel and floor lights now sport LED bulbs, and I fitted a modern radio as well, though I am considering having the original Buick Sonomatic AM/FM radio rebuilt to modern specs. I have a new fuel tank to replace the aged original, and there is some serious rocker panel and front fender support bracket rust damage to get repaired. Mike Sumrell The Aqua Zephyr receives plenty of honks and thumbs-ups when we take it out, and it is an eye-catching participant in the many car shows and cruise-ins we’ve attended over the years. It has also earned its fair share of first- and second-place awards. I spend a lot of time at shows talking to people about the car and the finer points of Rivieras in general, and one of the most common questions I get is “How do the headlights work?” Turning on the headlights rotates the light assemblies down until the bulbs are pointing through the rectangular front bumper openings. Turning the lights off rotates the lights skyward again. Most people who see this display are quite impressed. I have had the opportunity to buy other cars since purchasing the Aqua Zephyr, but my wife always reminds me that I don’t have room for more than one classic, and I’d have to sell the Buick to make room. Franky, I just can’t see myself parting with my Riviera any time soon! Mike Sumrell The post[Why, Yes, I Really Would Rather Have a Buick](https://www.hagerty.com/media/member-stories/why-yes-i-really-would-rather-have-a-buick/) appeared first on[Hagerty Media](https://www.hagerty.com/media) .
